tldr: We propose a humanoid control framework that fuses LiDAR and depth camera point clouds directly via voxelization without building maps, enabling a single reinforcement learning policy to traverse diverse challenging terrains such as 70-cm-high platforms and 100-cm gaps.
hero_caption: The life-sized humanoid DR02 traverses indoor settings—including 45-cm thin barriers, 100-cm gaps, 20-cm stairs, 70-cm platforms, stepping stones, and balance beams—as well as unseen outdoor surfaces one after another, all using the same trained policy.
overview:
For humanoid robots to operate safely in complex real-world environments like outdoor sites and industrial plants, they must reliably step across heterogeneous terrains, including narrow footholds, large elevation changes, and gaps. However, conventional vision-based locomotion control has major vulnerabilities. A single forward depth camera provides a narrow field of view. Height maps (2D grid representations of elevation around the robot) easily drift and distort under aggressive motion due to odometry drift, completely missing thin vertical barriers. Furthermore, directly processing multi-camera images with CNNs causes computational cost to scale with the number of cameras.

To overcome these issues, the authors developed "UniPoint," a humanoid locomotion framework that treats 3D measurements from a 360° LiDAR and two front/rear depth cameras as "simply 3D points" and early-fuses them directly in the robot base frame. Point clouds are voxelized and downsampled into a fixed number of tokens (400), which are then encoded using linear self-attention and proprioception-queried cross-attention. This captures omnidirectional terrain features while maintaining a constant computational cost, entirely without relying on map building or odometry.

Additionally, the framework introduces a reward design that densely penalizes foot-sole support violations in simulation, alongside a unified curriculum training protocol with sensor noise and dropout injection. Deployed directly on an onboard low-power processor (RK3588) of a real life-sized humanoid (1.75 m, 75 kg DR02) without any fine-tuning, the policy successfully ascends/descends 70-cm platforms, clears 100-cm gaps, and climbs stairs even with the LiDAR completely occluded.
contributions: Built an efficient, low-overhead perception pipeline that early-fuses measurements from a 360° LiDAR and front/rear depth cameras at the point-cloud level, processing them with a fixed token count decoupled from sensor count.

Substantially boosted stability on sparse footholds by introducing a foot-sole support-integrity scan reward that densely evaluates multi-point ground contact, paired with a slope-aligned velocity decomposition reward.
Trained a unified policy across eight diverse terrain types in a single training run via perception-degradation injection and domain randomization.
Demonstrated record-breaking real-world locomotion on a life-sized humanoid robot—including 70-cm platforms and 100-cm gaps—while maintaining an ultra-fast onboard inference time of 1.5 ms.

sections.heading: Why Were Humanoid "Eyes" So Unreliable in the Past?
sections.summary: Real-world outdoor deployment requires humanoids to traverse diverse terrains using whole-body locomotion, but conventional height-map and image-based methods struggle with narrow fields of view, state drift, and high computational costs. To break through these bottlenecks, UniPoint fuses multi-sensor measurements at the point-cloud level and processes them efficiently with a fixed token budget.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to perform practical inspections at electrical substations or factory maintenance sites, they must safely negotiate highly heterogeneous terrains: stairs, slopes, stepping stones, balance beams, and thin board-like barriers. Identifying secure footholds requires three capabilities simultaneously: wide coverage, local accuracy, and redundancy against sensor failure.

However, existing approaches suffer from structural limitations:
- Blind locomotion relying solely on proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.) is immune to visual sensor failure, but cannot anticipate terrain ahead of the feet, making discontinuous terrains like stepping stones impassable.
- A single forward depth camera or local height sampling around the robot leaves blind spots beneath the feet and behind the robot.
- Elevation maps updated via odometry tend to drift and distort under aggressive foot impacts or body swaying, and their 2D discretization critically misses thin vertical structures standing on the ground.
- Feeding multi-camera images directly into policy networks makes CNN inference costs scale linearly with the number of cameras.

UniPoint radically shifts perspective: range sensors are simply sources of 3D points. It aggregates point clouds from a 360° LiDAR and two depth cameras directly in the robot base frame, compressing them into a fixed number of tokens via voxelization. Because it creates neither maps nor images, it requires no odometry and decouples computation cost entirely from the sensor count.

sections.heading: Evolution of Perceptive Locomotion and the Point Cloud Interface
sections.summary: Humanoid locomotion research has evolved from blind locomotion via teacher-student learning to elevation maps and direct point-cloud processing. UniPoint extends these ideas, standing out with mapless early fusion at the point-cloud level combined with proprioception-queried cross-attention.
sections.details:
Recent reinforcement learning for humanoid locomotion can be categorized by how perceptual inputs are handled.

### II-A Learning-Based Humanoid Locomotion
With advancements in massively parallel simulation, distillation from a privileged teacher policy (with perfect simulation terrain info) to a student policy receiving only cameras or proprioception has become standard. Prior works such as DPL (using a single depth camera), RPL (distilling multiple cameras for forward/backward walking), and onboard foot-terrain reconstruction have made progress, but traversing diverse challenging obstacles with a single unified model remained unsolved.

### II-B Perceptive Locomotion and Terrain Representation
Elevation map reconstruction has been widely adopted as a terrain representation. However, even when LiDAR and depth cameras are fused, filtering through an elevation map still exposes the system to vanishing vertical walls and odometry drift. Conversely, directly feeding raw point clouds into policies via PointNet or voxelization has emerged in quadrupedal locomotion. UniPoint distinguishes itself by directly grouping multi-sensor points into a unified voxel token set and using proprioceptive queries to adaptively attend to critical spatial locations.

### II-C Safe Foot Placement and Reward Design
To cross sparse footholds like stepping stones or balance beams, reward design that prevents missteps is paramount. Because falling from a missed step provides a delayed, sparse signal, researchers have used multi-point foot sampling to provide dense penalties upon boundary violations. This work builds upon this concept, introducing a foot-sole support-integrity scan paired with a slope-aligned velocity decomposition curriculum.

sections.heading: Grouping Points and Reading with Attention: The UniPoint Architecture
sections.summary: LiDAR and depth point clouds are voxelized in the robot base frame and represented as 400 fixed tokens processed via linear self-attention and cross-attention. Combined with foot-sole scan rewards, slope velocity decomposition, and perception-degradation injection, a single PPO run yields exceptional robustness.
sections.details:
The complete UniPoint pipeline consists of point-cloud fusion, a specialized policy architecture, and robust simulation reward formulations.

### III-A Overview
The locomotion policy $\pi_{\theta}$ operates at 50 Hz, outputting target joint positions for 23 whole-body degrees of freedom (12 legs, 3 waist, 8 arms) tracked by PD controllers. Inputs consist of a 5-frame (~0.1 s) proprioceptive history, 400 voxel tokens, and velocity commands. Training uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in a single-stage end-to-end framework. It imposes no gait patterns, phase signals, or periodicity constraints; natural gaits emerge purely from rewards and the terrain curriculum.

### III-B Multi-Source Point-Level Perception Fusion
Point clouds from the head-mounted 360° LiDAR (20 Hz) and two torso-mounted depth cameras (60 Hz) first undergo self-collision filtering using a torso bounding box. The remaining points are quantized into a robot-centric $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ voxel grid, computing the centroid of each voxel. From these, $K=80$ tokens are randomly sampled and stacked across $G=5$ frames, producing $80 \times 5 = 400$ tokens. Each token carries a temporal positional encoding, allowing the policy to implicitly account for short-term ego-motion without explicit odometry frame transforms.
Inside the network, point tokens pass through two layers of linear self-attention, reducing computational complexity from $O(N^2 d)$ to $O(Nd^2)$. Next, a state vector $s_t$ derived from proprioception and velocity commands serves as the query for a 16-head cross-attention layer over the point features. This mechanism—asking "given my current posture, which spatial points matter most right now?"—enables precise foothold selection.

### III-C Terrain-Aware Reward Design
To enforce safe landings, two novel terrain-aware rewards are introduced:
- **Foot-sole support-integrity scan**: 21 virtual rays ($7 \times 3$ grid) project beneath each foot sole to measure deviation $d_{f,i}$ from the nominal contact plane. Deviations beyond $-0.11\,\mathrm{m}$ (stepping into empty space) or $+0.02\,\mathrm{m}$ (obstacle collision) are flagged as violation points, penalizing the stance foot densely.
- **Slope-aligned velocity decomposition**: The ground plane directly beneath the robot is fitted via least squares, projecting horizontal velocity commands onto the slope's tangent plane. This ensures natural, strain-free forward velocity tracking on inclines and declines.

### III-D Unified Training with Deployment-Grade Robustness
Using Isaac Lab across 4,096 parallel environments, the policy trains across an eight-terrain difficulty curriculum simultaneously. During training, perception-degradation injection adds Gaussian noise, random point dropout, outlier artifacts, LiDAR motion scan distortion, and self-occlusions. Coupled with aggressive domain randomization over actuator delays, mass, and friction, this achieves seamless zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Real-World and Simulation Benchmarks: Overcoming 70-cm Platforms and 100-cm Gaps
sections.summary: Extensive evaluations were conducted with the DR02 humanoid in simulation and the real world. UniPoint achieved a 94.6% average success rate across eight simulation terrains. On the physical robot, it executed ultra-fast 1.5-ms onboard inference on a low-power SoC while clearing 70-cm platforms, 100-cm gaps, and climbing stairs with the LiDAR blinded.
sections.details:
To validate the framework, experiments were conducted on the full-sized DR02 humanoid (1.75 m tall, ~75 kg, controlling 23 of its 31 degrees of freedom).

### IV-A Experimental Setup
Computation ran onboard on an RK3588 SoC (CPU). UniPoint achieved a forward-pass inference time of just $1.5\,\mathrm{ms}$, over 5× faster than the depth-image CNN baseline ($8.6\,\mathrm{ms}$). Even including preprocessing ($0.2\sim 0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$), it remains remarkably lightweight. Baselines included a blind proprioceptive policy, conventional height sampling, a depth-image CNN (without LiDAR), and a Concat variant replacing cross-attention with an MLP.

### IV-B Simulation Results
Across eight challenging terrains in simulation, UniPoint achieved a 94.6% average success rate, maintaining at least 79% on every single terrain. All other baselines plummeted below 70% on specific terrains.
- **Thin barriers**: Height sampling plummeted to an 18.0% success rate because top-down grid projections missed the thin profile, whereas UniPoint reached 99.8% by preserving 3D point structure.
- **Stepping stones**: While height sampling (67.0%) and the CNN baseline (62.8%) struggled, UniPoint scored 79.2%.
- **Ablations**: Removing the foot-sole scan reward dropped stepping-stone success from 79% to 68% and tripled the contact violation rate from 10% to 33%. Replacing cross-attention with feature concatenation dropped stepping stones to 69.3% and thin barriers to 89.5%, proving that querying points using proprioception is vital.
- **Sensor degradation tolerance**: When testing under escalating point dropout rates, UniPoint retained an 81% success rate even at 25% dropout, vastly outperforming baselines.

### IV-C Real-World Results
Twenty trials were conducted for each setting on the physical robot:
- The real-world height-map baseline managed simple stairs and slopes, but suffered catastrophic failures on 70-cm platforms (9/20), 100-cm gaps (4/20), stepping stones (2/20), and thin barriers (0/20) due to odometry drift and vibration.
- In contrast, UniPoint used a single policy without site-specific parameter tuning to conquer 70-cm platform climbs/descents (20/20), 100-cm gap crossings (19/20), 45-cm thin barrier hurdles (19/20), balance beams (17/20), and stepping stones (16/20). Rear coverage also enabled backward stair walking (18/20).
- **Single-modality loss test**: When the 360° LiDAR was completely blinded by a white bag—leaving only the two depth cameras—the robot steadily climbed 40-cm platforms and navigated 20-cm stairs.
- **Unseen outdoor generalization**: Deployed zero-shot without safety tethers across unseen outdoor terrains—including gravel roads, rocky trails, forest flagstones, and metal grate stairs—the policy transferred successfully.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: UniPoint unites odometry-free point-level early fusion, foot-sole support scan rewards, and perception-degradation simulation to achieve ultra-low compute overhead alongside exceptional mobility. Future directions include expanding perception range and integrating upper-body contact behaviors.
sections.details:
UniPoint's outstanding performance stems from three mutually reinforcing pillars:
1. Odometry-free point-level fusion prevents thin structures from vanishing and enables graceful performance degradation under partial sensor failure.
2. The foot-sole support scan transforms delayed, sparse fall signals into dense reward feedback, maximizing foothold accuracy on narrow contact surfaces.
3. Perception-degradation injection and domain randomization bridge the Sim-to-Real gap, enabling real-world deployment without fine-tuning.

In the current implementation, the perception range is configured to 1.3 m forward and 1.1 m backward; this reflects deliberate coverage choices rather than an algorithmic limit. Because the voxel token budget is fixed, point-cloud preprocessing scales only linearly with point count, keeping network compute costs perfectly constant.

Future research will focus on extending perception distance, optimizing voxel resolutions, supporting whole-body multi-contact motions and manipulation (such as grasping handrails), and integrating dynamic obstacle tracking in dynamic environments.

takeaways: Treating all range sensors simply as 3D point sources and bundling them via voxelization without building maps or rendering images offers an ultra-efficient, robust design paradigm.
2D grid elevation maps are critically vulnerable to odometry drift and miss thin barriers; preserving direct 3D point structures offers substantial structural advantages.
Proprioception-queried cross-attention enables dynamic extraction of critical foothold geometry tailored directly to the robot's momentary posture out of vast spatial input.
Aggressively injecting sensor noise and dropouts during training allows humanoid hardware to maintain stable locomotion even if primary sensors like LiDAR fail completely.
limitations: Perception range is currently focused on the near field (1.3 m forward, 1.1 m backward), which may require expansion for higher-speed running or large dynamic bounds.
A 0.1-m voxel size limits precision on extremely narrow obstacles or fine ground textures (reducing voxel size to 0.05 m incurs a significant compute tradeoff).
The current formulation assumes static terrain, leaving adaptation to moving obstacles and navigating past dynamic pedestrians as future work.
